newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Belgium welcomes EU Zaire aid, urges security force.
newsitem.headline: Belgium welcomes EU Zaire aid, urges security force.

text.p: Belgium welcomed on Friday the European Union's decision to produce a coordinated aid and diplomatic policy for central Africa's Great Lakes region but said an international force to secure the area was now vital.
"Foreign Minister Eric Derycke is particularly pleased about the fact that the European Union decided a "Common Action" on Friday," the foreign ministry said in a statement.
"Minister Derycke insists again on the rapid deployment of an international force for East Zaire in order to secure this humanitarian aid," it added.

European Union development ministers agreed on Friday to put up a further 169 million Ecus ($217 million) in humanitarian aid to help refugees in the bloodstained region where hundreds of thousands of refugees are on the move.
The European Commissioner responsible for humanitarian aid Joao De Deus Pinheiro said the Commission would draw up an overall action plan for the region in early December, as aid was not enough.

"The basic idea is that humanitarian aid is important but was not enough. The political situation is highly complex and if you want peace and stability in the region you have to address the whole puzzle," he told a news conference.
The ministers also agreed to ask the Western European Union, the EU's fledgling defence arm, to provide support for an eventual humanitarian aid effort the region.
Belgium, a former colonial power in the Great Lakes region, has offered to provide logistical support for any international security force but has refused to actually join such a force.
With hundreds of thousands of refugees suddenly on the move, the situation on the ground is changing daily.
Zaire, which initially said any such international military intervention had to be even-handed, has now said it is not needed at all.
Several potential contributors to the force have also begun to get cold feet over the force that is due to be under Canadian command.
Belgium has agreed to help the EU in promoting political dialogue between the various nations and factions in the region, and Development Minister Reginald Moreels is due to visit next week.

But the situation has been further complicated by the diplomatic isolation of Burundi where the army staged a political coup in July, installing Major Pierre Buyoya as president resulting in a land and air embargo of the country by its neighbours.
"We have agreed to act as facilitators. There are bilateral contacts taking place...trying to gradually bring all sides closer together," a foreign ministry spokesman said earlier this week.

But Africa specialists note that such is the tangled history of ethnic enmity and suspicion in the region that each time one faction feels it is getting the upper hand it simply stops talking to the others.
